article.title: The Critical Spare Parts List: The Shelf That Turns a Breakdown Into an Annoyance
article.body_markdown:
The preventive maintenance schedule stops most failures. This page covers the ones that happen anyway — because the difference between a breakdown and an outage is usually not skill and not luck; it is whether the part that failed was already on a shelf you own. An OEM with an eleven-day lead time does not care that your machine stopped on day one of your biggest contract. The shelf is the only supplier whose lead time you control.

**The list is five columns, built from the maintenance log in one afternoon with the person who actually fixes things:** the part (named as the floor names it, with the manufacturer part number written next to it — "the little green board in the cabinet" is how a 2 a.m. order does not get placed); what it gates (not "lathe" — "lathe → the aerospace lot due the 14th, $31k"); source and **real** lead time (the last time you bought it, how long did it actually take?); shelf quantity with a two-bin reorder point (one bin in use, one sealed; empty bin goes on the purchase bench, not back on the shelf); and last-used, which feeds the kill list.

**The 48-hour rule decides what belongs on the shelf:** if the part gates revenue and its real lead time is longer than you can tolerate the machine being down, it belongs on the shelf. A two-day lead on a machine you can live without for a week — order on demand. A three-week factory lead on the machine that produces your payroll — that is the shelf. Cost is the tiebreaker, not the gate: a $340 drive that saves a $180k contract is not a $340 part, it is cheap insurance with a part number.

**A shelf with no reorder point is a battery that drains silently.** The first spare you use feels free; the point of the list is that using a spare *starts an order*, not that using a spare was possible. The worst version of a spare is the one you used in March and remembered in September — empty shelf, long lead, breakdown twice.

**The kill list runs once a year with the last-used column open.** Spares for retired machines, superseded revisions, anything untouched for two years: sell it, return it, scrap it — get it off the shelf and its value back into the business. One shop's audit found sixty-two spares; eighteen belonged to machines retired before the current owner bought the company. Dead stock: $2,100.

**Five traps:** buying spares for everything (the list exists to rank; spares for every part of every machine is capital that sleeps); the spare for the machine that left (shelves drift — the last-used column and the annual walk are the fix); no reorder point (two-bin or min-max, reordered the day the bin empties, not the day someone remembers); **untested spares** (the drive never powered up, the seal that does not fit the revision you actually run — a part-shaped hope; fit-check on the maintenance cadence); and spares without the fiche (manual, torque spec, wiring diagram, config backup stored *with* the part — otherwise the shelf serves whoever remembers, and the person who remembers is on leave the week it fails).

**The worked example:** a twelve-person CNC machine shop ran production through one 1998 vertical machining centre — it held tolerance like nothing else they could afford to replace. The servo drive died mid-way through an aerospace lot worth $180k with a delivery penalty attached. OEM quote: eleven days. The owner had heard this exact story from a neighbouring shop eighteen months earlier — same machine class, same failure, same eleven-day quote, a lost batch and a lost customer — and had spent one afternoon building this list from that neighbour's expensive education.

The shelf had the drive: $340, bought eight months earlier, bin-and-seal. The fiche was in the same drawer — parameter sheet, torque specs, configuration backup on a labelled USB stick. Forty minutes from dark machine to spindle turning. The lot shipped on time and the penalty clause never woke. The same walk caught a $140 fuse kit wound for the old spindle motor (replaced, fit-checked) and eleven spares for a bandsaw scrapped in 2023, sold to the scrap dealer's parts counter for $410 — dead stock out, coffee money in.

The shelf is not a cost. You are not buying parts; you are buying back lead time you do not control — at shelf prices instead of penalty prices.

**The full page** — with the five columns in detail, the 48-hour rule, the traps, and the worked example — lives at [Hive Ops Notes](https://hive80-lab.github.io/ops-notes/critical-spare-parts-list.html).

article.description: Five columns from the maintenance log: what the part gates, source and real lead time, two-bin reorder point, last used. The 48-hour rule for what belongs on the shelf — plus the CNC shop whose $340 drive answered an eleven-day OEM lead mid-way through a $180k lot.
